questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-material living standard?
options: The quality of the natural environment
Real household disposable income per person
The quantity of goods and services consumed per person
Real GDP per capita
questions.explanation: Non-material living standards are aspects of wellbeing that cannot easily be bought, such as environmental quality, health, safety and literacy. Incomes, consumption and real GDP per capita measure material living standards.

questions.stem: Rising real GDP per capita is an imperfect measure of living standards because it:
options: counts the output of goods but leaves out the output of services entirely
excludes all spending by government on goods and services such as health
ignores non-material factors such as leisure, health and environmental quality
is not adjusted for changes in the general level of prices over the period
questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita measures average output and income, but says nothing about leisure, the environment or how income is shared. It is already adjusted for price changes and includes services and government spending.

questions.stem: Rising crime rates in a city are most likely to reduce:
options: material living standards, by raising spending on locks and security
non-material living standards, by reducing people's sense of safety
material living standards only, by lowering the measured value of real GDP
neither kind of living standard, because crime is not counted in GDP at all
questions.explanation: Crime affects wellbeing through fear and loss of safety, which are non-material living standards. Extra spending on security would actually add to measured GDP rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: Rapid expansion of mining raises real incomes in a region but increases dust pollution and respiratory illness. The best assessment is that:
options: material living standards fall, as more household income is spent on healthcare
neither changes, as the gains in income and the costs in health cancel exactly
material living standards rise while non-material living standards may fall
both material and non-material living standards must rise with higher incomes
questions.explanation: Higher real incomes raise access to goods and services, lifting material living standards. Worse air quality and health are costs to non-material living standards, so growth can raise one while lowering the other.

questions.stem: In the five-sector circular flow model, the three leakages are:
options: consumption, saving and investment
taxation, transfer payments and exports
saving, taxation and imports
investment, government spending and exports
questions.explanation: Leakages are flows of income that are not spent on domestic production: saving, taxation and imports. Investment, government spending and exports are injections into the flow.

questions.stem: In the five-sector circular flow model, which of the following is an injection?
options: Spending by Australian tourists on hotels while travelling overseas
Spending by overseas students on tuition at Australian universities
Households placing part of their weekly income in bank deposits
Taxes paid by Australian companies on the profits they earn
questions.explanation: Overseas students' spending on Australian education is an export of services, which injects spending into the domestic flow. Saving and taxes are leakages, and Australians' spending overseas is an import, also a leakage.

questions.stem: If total injections exceed total leakages in the circular flow, the level of economic activity will tend to:
options: fall, as more spending leaves the flow than is added to it
stay the same, as injections and leakages always balance in every period
rise, because households are choosing to save more of their income
rise, as more spending is added to the flow than leaves it
questions.explanation: When injections such as investment, government spending and exports exceed leakages, total spending on domestic output grows and activity expands. Higher saving would be a leakage, which works the other way.

questions.stem: In the five-sector circular flow model, the main role of financial institutions is to:
options: channel household saving into loans for business investment and other borrowers
collect taxes from households and firms and pay transfer payments to households
buy goods and services from overseas producers on behalf of Australian households
produce goods and services, paying households wages, rent, interest and profit
questions.explanation: Financial institutions take in saving, a leakage, and lend it to firms and households who spend it, so saving can return to the flow as investment. Collecting taxes is the government sector's role, and production is the role of firms.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical economy, saving is $40 billion, taxation $60 billion, imports $50 billion, investment $45 billion, government spending $55 billion and exports $40 billion. What is likely to happen to economic activity?
options: It rises, as injections exceed leakages by $10 billion
It is stable, as leakages and injections are equal
It falls, as leakages exceed injections by $5 billion
It falls, as leakages exceed injections by $10 billion
questions.explanation: Leakages total 40 + 60 + 50 = $150 billion and injections total 45 + 55 + 40 = $140 billion. With $10 billion more leaving the flow than entering it, total spending and economic activity fall.

questions.stem: In the circular flow model, households provide firms with the factors of production. In return, households receive:
options: income such as wages, rent, interest and profit
transfer payments such as the age pension
goods and services imported from overseas
the taxation revenue collected by government
questions.explanation: Households own land, labour, capital and enterprise and sell their services to firms in exchange for factor incomes. Transfer payments come from government, not from firms in exchange for factors.

questions.stem: The term 'business cycle' describes:
options: the stages a single firm passes through from its start-up to its closure
the flow of money between households and firms
the yearly cycle of government budget decisions
fluctuations in the level of economic activity over time around its trend
questions.explanation: The business cycle describes the recurring expansions and contractions in economic activity, measured mainly by real GDP growth, around the long-run trend. It is an economy-wide pattern, not the life cycle of a single firm.

questions.stem: During the contraction phase of the business cycle, the most likely combination is:
options: slowing real GDP growth, falling unemployment and rising inflation
rising unemployment, rising inflation and stronger business confidence
slowing real GDP growth, rising unemployment and easing inflation
faster real GDP growth, falling unemployment and rising inflation
questions.explanation: In a contraction, spending and output grow more slowly or fall, firms need fewer workers, and spare capacity reduces pressure on prices. Rising inflation and falling unemployment are features of an expansion.

questions.stem: A common definition of a recession is:
options: any year in which inflation falls below the target band
any year in which the federal budget is in deficit
two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
two consecutive quarters of rising unemployment
questions.explanation: A technical recession is commonly defined as two quarters in a row in which real GDP shrinks. Unemployment usually rises in a recession, but it is not the defining measure.

questions.stem: At the peak of the business cycle, the economy is most likely to show:
options: low unemployment, capacity constraints and rising inflationary pressure
high unemployment and large amounts of spare productive capacity
falling prices and weak business confidence
negative real GDP growth and rising cyclical unemployment
questions.explanation: At a peak, demand is pressing against the economy's capacity, so unemployment is low and firms struggle to meet demand, which pushes up prices. High unemployment and spare capacity are features of a trough.

questions.stem: A sharp fall in business and consumer confidence occurs, with no change in the economy's productive capacity. This is most likely to cause:
options: a fall in aggregate supply that pushes the inflation rate higher
an expansion, as households save more and banks lend more
higher inflation, as households bring their spending forward
a downturn in the business cycle as aggregate demand falls
questions.explanation: Lower confidence leads households and firms to cut consumption and investment, reducing aggregate demand and slowing growth. Productive capacity is unchanged, so this is a demand-side cause of the downturn rather than a supply shock.

questions.stem: Aggregate demand is best defined as:
options: total planned spending on Australian-produced goods and services, C + I + G + (X − M)
the total output the economy could produce with all its resources fully employed
total spending by households on consumer goods and services over a year
the total value of Australia's imports and exports over a year
questions.explanation: Aggregate demand is the total spending on domestically produced output by households, firms, government and overseas buyers, less spending on imports. Total potential output is a supply-side concept.

questions.stem: A rise in interest rates is most likely to reduce aggregate demand by:
options: raising the disposable income of households with variable-rate mortgages
making Australian exports cheaper for overseas buyers to purchase
increasing the incentive for firms to borrow and invest in new capital
discouraging borrowing for household consumption and business investment
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, so households and firms spend less. They reduce, rather than raise, the disposable income of mortgage holders.

questions.stem: A depreciation of the Australian dollar is likely to increase aggregate demand because:
options: exports become cheaper overseas and imports dearer at home, raising net exports
imports become cheaper for Australians, encouraging more household consumption
foreign currency debt becomes cheaper to service, raising business investment
overseas interest rates fall, so Australian firms borrow more from abroad
questions.explanation: A lower dollar makes Australian goods cheaper for foreign buyers and imports dearer for Australians, so X rises and M falls. A depreciation makes imports dearer, not cheaper, and raises the cost of servicing foreign currency debt.

questions.stem: Strong economic growth in Australia's major trading partners is most likely to:
options: increase Australian aggregate supply by lowering local production costs
lower aggregate demand as Australians buy more imports from those partners
raise demand for Australian exports, increasing aggregate demand
reduce demand for Australian exports as partners produce more themselves
questions.explanation: Faster growth abroad lifts incomes overseas, so foreign buyers purchase more Australian exports. Higher exports add directly to aggregate demand.

questions.stem: A cut in personal income tax rates affects aggregate demand mainly by:
options: raising household disposable income and therefore consumption
lowering business costs of production and so raising aggregate supply
reducing the exchange rate and so raising Australia's net exports
raising interest rates and so lowering business investment spending
questions.explanation: Lower income tax leaves households with more disposable income, and much of it is spent, raising consumption. Income tax is paid by households, so the main effect is on demand rather than on business costs.

questions.stem: Business confidence rises strongly while consumer confidence is unchanged. The component of aggregate demand most directly affected is:
options: consumption, as households increase their spending
government spending, as tax revenue rises with profits
imports, which fall as firms buy more from local suppliers
investment, as firms expand their productive capacity
questions.explanation: Business confidence drives firms' decisions to invest in new capital, so the investment component rises. Consumer confidence, which drives household consumption, has not changed.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply is best defined as:
options: the total output producers are willing and able to supply at each price level
total planned spending on goods and services by every sector of the economy
the value of Australia's exports less the value of its imports
the stock of machinery and buildings owned by firms
questions.explanation: Aggregate supply is the total quantity of goods and services the economy's producers will supply at different price levels. Total planned spending is aggregate demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to increase aggregate supply?
options: A widespread drought across eastern Australia
Disruption to international shipping routes
Productivity growth as firms adopt new technology
A sharp rise in global oil prices
questions.explanation: Productivity growth lets firms produce more with the same inputs, lowering costs and raising aggregate supply. Oil price rises, drought and shipping disruption all raise costs or cut output, reducing aggregate supply.

questions.stem: A large rise in the price of imported fuel is most likely to:
options: increase aggregate supply, as fuel importers earn more from each sale
increase aggregate demand, as households spend more on fuel than before
decrease aggregate supply, lowering the price level and reducing output
decrease aggregate supply, raising the price level and reducing real output
questions.explanation: Fuel is an input into most production, so a rise in its price raises costs and reduces aggregate supply. A fall in aggregate supply pushes the price level up while output falls.

questions.stem: Disruptions to international supply chains affect aggregate supply mainly by:
options: raising the quality of the domestic labour force over time
raising costs and causing shortages of imported inputs
increasing overseas demand for Australian exports
lowering domestic interest rates for business borrowers
questions.explanation: When shipping and supply routes are disrupted, firms face delays and higher prices for parts and materials, which raises costs and limits output. That reduces aggregate supply.

questions.stem: A depreciation of the Australian dollar can reduce aggregate supply because it:
options: raises the cost of imported inputs such as fuel and machinery
makes Australian exports less competitive in overseas markets
lowers the cost of servicing debt borrowed in foreign currencies
increases the participation rate of the domestic labour force
questions.explanation: A lower dollar raises the Australian dollar price of imported inputs, increasing costs for firms that use them. A depreciation makes exports more competitive, and raises rather than lowers the cost of foreign currency debt.

questions.stem: New government regulations that add to firms' compliance costs are likely to:
options: increase aggregate supply by lowering costs of production
increase the economy's productive capacity over time
decrease aggregate demand by raising interest rates
decrease aggregate supply by raising costs of production
questions.explanation: Compliance costs are a cost of production, so heavier regulation reduces the output firms will supply at each price level. Aggregate supply decreases.

questions.stem: Which change raises aggregate supply through the quality, rather than the quantity, of the factors of production?
options: More land brought into agricultural production
An increase in the participation rate of older workers
A better-trained workforce from improved vocational education
A rise in the working-age population through migration
questions.explanation: Training raises the skills and productivity of each worker, which is an improvement in quality. Migration, more land and higher participation increase the quantity of resources available.

questions.stem: Real GDP growth rises while the inflation rate falls. Which change best explains both movements?
options: An increase in aggregate demand
A decrease in aggregate supply
A decrease in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate supply
questions.explanation: An increase in aggregate supply raises output while easing pressure on prices. An increase in aggregate demand would raise output but push inflation up, and a decrease in demand would slow both.

questions.stem: Inflation rises while real GDP growth slows. The most likely cause is:
options: a fall in aggregate demand, caused by weaker growth overseas
a fall in aggregate supply, such as a sharp rise in energy costs
a rise in aggregate demand, driven by stronger consumer confidence
a rise in aggregate supply, driven by faster productivity growth
questions.explanation: Rising prices together with slower growth is the signature of a supply shock. A demand increase would raise both growth and inflation, while a demand fall would lower both.

questions.stem: The rate of economic growth is measured as:
options: the percentage change in nominal GDP over a period
the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index
the percentage change in the population over a period
the percentage change in real GDP over a period
questions.explanation: Economic growth is the rate of increase in real GDP, the volume of goods and services produced. Nominal GDP also rises with prices, so it overstates growth in output when there is inflation.

questions.stem: Economists use real rather than nominal GDP to measure economic growth because real GDP:
options: excludes government spending, which does not add to the economy's output
is divided by the population, giving the change in output for each person
removes the effect of price changes, showing the change in the volume of output
includes non-material living standards such as leisure and environmental quality
questions.explanation: Real GDP is nominal GDP adjusted for inflation, so it shows how much more is actually being produced. Dividing by population gives real GDP per capita, which is a different measure.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical economy, real GDP rises from $2400 billion to $2460 billion over a year. The rate of economic growth is:
options: 5.0 per cent
2.4 per cent
0.25 per cent
2.5 per cent
questions.explanation: Growth is (2460 − 2400) ÷ 2400 × 100 = 2.5 per cent. Dividing the $60 billion increase by the new level of $2460 billion gives about 2.4 per cent, which uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: Over a year, nominal GDP grows by 7 per cent and the general price level rises by 4.5 per cent. Real GDP grew by approximately:
options: 2.5 per cent
11.5 per cent
1.6 per cent
4.5 per cent
questions.explanation: Real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation: 7 − 4.5 = 2.5 per cent. Adding the two figures together would treat price rises as extra output.

questions.stem: Real GDP grows by 2 per cent while the population grows by 2.5 per cent. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP per capita rises by about 4.5 per cent
Real GDP per capita rises by about 0.5 per cent
Real GDP per capita is unchanged, as both rose
Real GDP per capita falls by about 0.5 per cent
questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita changes by roughly the growth in real GDP minus the growth in population: 2 − 2.5 = −0.5 per cent. Output grew, but not as fast as the number of people sharing it.

questions.stem: The goal of strong and sustainable economic growth means growth that is:
options: fast enough to lift living standards without causing inflation, external or environmental problems
as fast as possible each year, regardless of its effects on prices or the environment
equal to the average growth rate of Australia's major trading partners each year
driven mainly by government spending rather than by private consumption and investment
questions.explanation: The goal is the highest rate of growth that can be maintained over time without pushing up inflation, worsening external accounts or degrading the environment. Growing as fast as possible regardless of those effects is not sustainable.

questions.stem: Growth well above the economy's sustainable rate is most likely to cause:
options: rising inflation as demand outstrips productive capacity
rising cyclical unemployment as firms cut their workforces
falling spending on imports as domestic incomes grow faster
falling tax revenue as household and company incomes rise
questions.explanation: When spending grows faster than the economy's capacity, firms cannot keep up and raise prices, so inflation rises. Fast growth lowers rather than raises cyclical unemployment and tends to increase imports and tax revenue.

questions.stem: Rapid growth in domestic spending can create external pressures for Australia because:
options: foreign debt falls when national income is growing faster than overseas
trading partners respond to strong Australian growth by cutting their interest rates
spending on imports rises, which worsens the current account balance
export volumes rise automatically whenever domestic spending grows faster
questions.explanation: Higher domestic incomes and spending draw in more imports, so the current account balance deteriorates. Exports depend mainly on overseas demand, not on domestic spending.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of growth that is not environmentally sustainable?
options: Output growth from clearing native vegetation faster than it regenerates
Output growth from improved labour productivity in service industries
Output growth from using energy more efficiently in manufacturing
Output growth from recycled materials replacing newly mined inputs
questions.explanation: Clearing vegetation faster than it can regrow uses up natural capital, reducing future living standards. Growth from productivity, energy efficiency or recycling uses resources more carefully.

questions.stem: If economic growth stays below its sustainable rate for a long period, the most likely outcome is:
options: rising unemployment as firms need fewer workers
rising inflation as firms raise their prices
worsening shortages of skilled labour across industries
rising tax revenue as household incomes grow faster than expected
questions.explanation: Weak growth means less output and less demand for labour, so cyclical unemployment rises. Inflationary pressure and skill shortages are associated with growth that is too fast, not too slow.
